messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 34
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Navy Officer
- Trauma Type: Natural disaster
- Pcl5: 33

**Vignette: Marcus, 34**

Marcus has always understood the sea. He grew up near the water in coastal Virginia, joined the Navy at eighteen, and spent the better part of his adult life reading weather systems, navigating open ocean, and trusting that preparation could outpace catastrophe. That belief held until the summer two years ago, when his vessel was stationed off the Gulf Coast and Hurricane Ida made landfall with a fury that no amount of training had truly prepared him for.

The storm arrived faster than the updated models had projected. Marcus was on deck coordinating the securing of equipment when the surge hit — a wall of water that took out two junior sailors and pinned him against a steel railing for what he later learned was nearly four minutes. He remembers the sound most vividly: not wind, but a deep, pressurized roar, like the ocean had turned inside out. He was pulled to safety by a petty officer. The two sailors survived, though one sustained serious injuries. Marcus walked away with bruised ribs and a laceration along his left forearm that required sixteen stitches. On paper, he was fine.

He returned to duty within the week. There was paperwork, a brief medical clearance, and the quiet expectation that officers absorb difficulty and move forward. Marcus did what he had always done — he moved forward. He told his wife, Dana, that it had been a close call, nothing more.

But the nights told a different story. For months after the storm, Marcus would wake between two and four in the morning, chest tight, convinced he could hear that pressurized roar somewhere outside the bedroom window. He would lie still for long minutes, cataloguing sounds — the hum of the refrigerator, Dana's breathing, a car passing on the street — until he could locate himself in the present. He rarely went back to sleep.

At work, he began struggling in ways that confused him. He is a methodical, respected officer, someone his crew describes as unflappable. But during a training exercise six months after the incident, when an unexpected squall rolled in, he found himself frozen at the helm for nearly thirty seconds — an eternity in his world. He covered it, barked an order, and no one seemed to notice. He noticed. He started reviewing weather reports compulsively before every deployment, sometimes checking the same forecast four or five times in an hour.

At home, Dana has noticed a flatness in him that she struggles to name. He is present but not quite there — engaged enough at dinner, patient with their seven-year-old daughter, but somehow behind glass. He has stopped taking his daughter to the beach, offering rotating excuses. He has not told Dana why. There is a part of him that believes if he says it aloud — that standing near open water now fills him with a dread he cannot rationalize — it will mean something is permanently wrong with him.

He does not think of himself as someone who was traumatized. He thinks of himself as someone who had a bad day at sea and has not quite gotten his footing back. He uses that language carefully, because the other language feels like a door he is not ready to open. He is aware, in a clinical corner of his mind, that something shifted that day on the deck. He is aware that the man who believed preparation could outpace catastrophe no longer fully believes that. He grieves that loss quietly, the way he grieves most things — privately, and without much ceremony.

He came to therapy at Dana's gentle insistence, framing it initially as stress management. In sessions, he is thoughtful and articulate, precise in the way officers often are. He chooses his words carefully. But occasionally, when describing the sound of the water, he goes quiet for a moment longer than usual, and his hands, resting on his knees, press down just slightly, as if steadying himself against something only he can feel.
